practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: A 'toolchain' is the full chain of tools code passes through before you see a result - editor, terminal, runtime. Verifying it means proving every link works, not hoping it does.
hints: Run `node -v` and `npm -v` as two separate commands and read each output before moving on.
`first-run.js` only needs `console.log(...)` lines - resist adding anything more complex.
commonMistakes: Running `node -v` in a different terminal tab than `node first-run.js`, then being confused when results seem inconsistent.
debuggingChecklist: Confirm the terminal prompt shows you inside the project folder before running anything.
Re-run `node -v` alone if the file fails, to isolate whether Node or your file is the problem.
thinkingPrompts: If `node first-run.js` printed nothing, would that mean the file is empty, or that it errored before your first console.log?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a line printing the current date via `new Date()`, and explain in the README what type of value that is.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every professional onboarding starts with exactly this: verify the toolchain before writing any product code.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: Most learners rush this one. Don't. A verified toolchain is the cheapest insurance you'll buy all bootcamp.

practicalMissions.helpPromptTemplate: I am on Week {weekNumber}, Mission {missionNumber} of the XcelerateAI Bootcamp. I am trying to build {missionTitle}. I created these files: {filesCreated}. The error I got is: {errorMessage}. I have tried: {attempts}. Please help me debug this without giving me the full answer immediately.
practicalMissions.background: A 'mission log' here is just a structured console report - the same pattern you'll use later for API responses and debug output, with plain variables instead of network data.
hints: Template literals (`` `Hello ${name}` ``) read far better than chaining `+` between strings.
If a printed value shows `undefined`, the variable was declared but never assigned - or assigned after it printed.
commonMistakes: Believing a variable updates everywhere automatically after you change it once, rather than re-running the prints that reference it.
debuggingChecklist: Check for a missing closing quote or backtick on the exact line the error names.
Confirm every variable used in a print was declared above it, not below.
thinkingPrompts: Why might five separate single-purpose print lines be more debuggable than one giant combined string?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Turn the five print lines into a single multi-line template literal report and compare readability.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Structured status logging is exactly what you'll use to debug a backend server in Month 4 when there's no UI to look at.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: The debugging drill here - deleting a quote on purpose - is the highest-value habit in this whole mission.

practicalMissions.background: This mission has no new syntax - it exists purely to make 'proof of work' a habit, not an afterthought tacked onto the end of a project.
hints: A README doesn't need to be long - it needs to let a stranger run your code without asking one question.
`git status` before and after `git add`/`commit` is the fastest way to build intuition for what each command does.
commonMistakes: Writing a README that describes what the code does conceptually but never states the exact command to run it.
debuggingChecklist: Does your README include the literal `node filename.js` command, copy-pasteable?
Did `git status` show 'nothing to commit' after committing, confirming it saved?
thinkingPrompts: If you reopened this repo in a year with no memory of it, could your README alone get you running in under two minutes?
practicalMissions.stretchChallenge: Add a `.gitignore` file and explain in the README why it's there, even with nothing to ignore yet.
practicalMissions.realWorldApplications: Every employer and client reads your README and commit history before running your code - this is the actual first impression.
practicalMissions.commanderNotes: This is the smallest mission of the week and the one that matters most for your portfolio's first impression.

weeks.scenario: Before Elliot can be a product, it has to be a file that runs. This week is about proving your machine is a real cockpit: you can create a file, make the computer execute it, read what it tells you back, and save that proof somewhere permanent. Every professional workflow you'll ever use - debugging, testing, deploying - depends on this loop working reliably first.
learningObjectives: Install and verify VS Code, Node.js, and Git
Use an integrated terminal inside VS Code
Create and run a JavaScript file with node
Read a terminal error and locate the line it points to
Initialize a Git repository and push a first commit
weeks.expectedOutcome: A GitHub repository containing at least two runnable JavaScript files and a README that explains, in your own words, how to set up and run them.
stretchGoals: Add a package.json with a `start` script so the project runs with `npm start`.
Write a version of first-run.js that reads a value from a command-line argument (`process.argv`).
hints: If `node -v` or `npm -v` prints nothing, the terminal you opened predates the install - close and reopen VS Code's terminal.
VS Code's integrated terminal starts in your open folder - you rarely need `cd` if you opened the right folder with `code .`.
`console.log` is not the only way to see a value - the bare Node REPL (`node` with no filename) prints any expression you type.
commonMistakes: Assuming a terminal error means the whole toolchain is broken, rather than reading which specific file and line it points to.
Believing 'the file exists in the folder' is the same as 'the terminal is currently inside that folder'.
Treating the first successful console.log as proof the setup is solid, without ever deliberately breaking something to see a real failure.
debugChecklist: Is the terminal's current folder the same folder the file is saved in?
Did you save the file before running it?
Is the exact filename typed correctly, including `.js`?
Does the error name a line number - have you opened that exact line?
Does `node -v` alone still work, confirming Node itself is fine?
thinkingPrompts: What actually happens when you type `node first-run.js` - what program reads your file, and what does it do with it?
If a teammate said 'it doesn't work,' what three questions would you ask before touching their code?
recallPrompts: Without looking it up, what command checks your installed Node.js version?
What is the difference between `git add` and `git commit`?
weeks.missionReview: This week had one real goal disguised as three missions: prove you can create, run, break, read, fix, and save code - reliably, not by luck. If you can already picture doing that loop again on a harder problem without panicking, Week 1 did its job.
weeks.progressNotes: Slow, careful terminal work now is what makes Month 4's backend server and Month 6's full Elliot assembly feel routine instead of terrifying - you're building muscle memory, not just a file.
weeks.missionDebrief: Environment confirmed. Toolchain verified. Your first commits are on GitHub and they will still be there in six months when Elliot V1 ships - that repository is now part of your permanent professional record.
weeks.commanderNotes: Every learner who finished this bootcamp started exactly where you are: a blank folder and a terminal that feels unfamiliar. The terminal stops feeling strange around week three. Keep the error messages - they're more useful than they feel right now.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week Elliot gets an identity: names, goals, and numbers stored in variables you control. The terminal skills you just built are about to start feeling routine.
reflectionPrompts: Walk through, step by step, everything that happens between typing `node first-run.js` and seeing output. Where could that chain break?
What is the difference between code that runs and code you can actually explain? Which do you have right now?
What exact error message did you deliberately cause this week, and what did it teach you about reading errors?
If a friend asked 'what did you actually build this week,' what would you show them first, and why?
What one habit from this week (terminal use, Git, reading errors) do you most want to keep doing on purpose?

weeks.scenario: Elliot's very first piece of real memory is small: a name, a role, a goal, a number of hours. Variables and types are how any program holds onto a fact instead of losing it the instant execution moves on. This week you build the smallest possible working memory system and prove you understand exactly what kind of value lives inside it.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with let and const and explain when to use each
Identify the type of any value
Use arithmetic operators to calculate derived values
Build multi-line output using template literals
Explain, with an example, what type coercion is and why it causes bugs
weeks.expectedOutcome: Three small working programs - a personal profile card, a real bootcamp-hours calculator, and a multi-line string report - each pushed to GitHub with a README.
stretchGoals: Add a variable holding an array of your goals and print its length in the profile report.
Use `typeof` on every variable in the Profile Data Card and print each type next to its value.
hints: `const` should be your default - reach for `let` only when a value genuinely needs to change.
If a calculation prints `NaN`, a number got treated as text somewhere upstream - trace backward to where the value was created.
commonMistakes: Believing `let` and `var` are interchangeable, when only `let`/`const` should be used.
Assuming a number in quotes (`"25"`) behaves like a real number (`25`) in a calculation.
Thinking a variable stores the expression used to create it, rather than the single computed value that resulted.
debugChecklist: Print the `typeof` of any value producing unexpected output.
Check whether a number came from input, a template literal, or concatenation - all can silently produce text.
Confirm every variable in a calculation is declared before it runs.
thinkingPrompts: If Elliot needs 'weekly hours' to calculate a six-month total, what type must it be, and what breaks if it were text?
Why might `const` reduce bugs compared to always defaulting to `let`?
recallPrompts: What are the three primitive types you used this week?
What symbol wraps an embedded expression inside a template literal?
weeks.missionReview: By now you've watched output change simply because a stored value changed - that's the entire point of variables, and the exact mechanism React state (Month 3) and a database record (Month 4) both build on.
weeks.progressNotes: If the hours math or template literals felt slower than Week 1, that's expected - you're doing real reasoning now, not just proving the toolchain works.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's identity data now exists as real, typed, calculable information. Every later mission that says 'store the user's X' is a variant of exactly what you just built.
weeks.commanderNotes: If `NaN` showed up anywhere this week, good - it's the single most instructive bug in JavaScript, and you now know what causes it.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week, Elliot starts making decisions. Everything you stored this week becomes something a function can check and respond to.
reflectionPrompts: Pick one variable from this week. What type is it, and what would break if it were the wrong type?
Where did `NaN` or `undefined` show up for you, and what did tracing it back teach you?
Elliot needs to remember your weekly hours accurately for six months. What did the Hours Calculator teach you about trusting stored data?
What's the real difference between `let` and `const` in your own words - not the textbook definition?
Which of the three missions could you rebuild from a blank file, and which not? Why?

weeks.scenario: An assistant that can only print is a script. An assistant that can decide is closer to a product. This week Elliot gets its first real decisions: given a situation (progress, blockers, deadline), what should it say back? Conditionals give it branches; functions give it reusable, testable logic instead of one tangled script.
learningObjectives: Write multi-branch decisions with if / else if / else
Distinguish a function declaration from an expression
Write functions that accept parameters and return a value
Explain why a returned value is more reusable than a printed one
Combine functions and conditionals into one decision flow
weeks.expectedOutcome: A working Elliot Response Engine that accepts different input combinations and returns different, correct, assistant-style advice for each.
stretchGoals: Add a fourth function that combines the other three's outputs into one formatted paragraph.
Replace one if/else chain with a switch statement and compare readability.
hints: Write the plain-English decision first before typing any code.
A function that only uses `console.log` and never `return`s is usually doing the caller's job for it.
commonMistakes: Using `=` where `===` was intended inside a condition - this week's drill exists to make that visible once.
Believing a function 'runs itself' when defined, without realizing it must be called.
Confusing what a function prints with what it returns.
debugChecklist: If a condition never triggers, check for a single `=` instead of `===`.
If a result is `undefined` where you expected a value, check for a missing `return`.
Trace a decision by hand with real values before assuming the logic is wrong.
thinkingPrompts: Given three outcomes (Ready / Almost Ready / Blocked), what is the minimum number of conditions to separate all three?
Why might returning a value be better than printing inside a reusable function?
recallPrompts: What is the difference between `=` and `===`?
Name one difference between a function declaration and a function expression.
weeks.missionReview: You've now written code that makes a real decision based on real conditions - the conceptual seed of every 'if the user is logged in, show X' pattern you'll write for the rest of the bootcamp.
weeks.progressNotes: If the Boss Drill took longer than the other two missions, that's expected - it deliberately combines everything from the whole week into one flow.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot can now reason about a situation and respond differently. That is, functionally, the smallest definition of 'intelligent behavior' - built from three plain functions and some if statements.
weeks.commanderNotes: The `=` vs `===` bug you triggered is one every professional has shipped to production at least once. Recognizing it fast is a real skill.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week, Elliot needs to hold more than one thing at a time - multiple goals, projects, notes. Arrays and objects are how real data collections get modeled.
reflectionPrompts: Describe, in plain English, the exact decision logic your Readiness Checker makes - could someone follow it without your code?
What's the difference between a function that prints and one that returns? Where did that matter this week?
You caused an `=` vs `===` bug this week. What made it hard or easy to spot?
Which of your three assistant functions would be easiest to reuse elsewhere, and why?
If Elliot needed a fourth decision category next month, how would you extend this week's logic without rewriting it?

concepts: Combining arrays, objects, functions, and conditionals
weeks.scenario: A real assistant doesn't manage one goal or project - it manages many, in a structure it can search and update. This week Elliot gets a real memory shape: arrays for lists, objects for the details of any one thing, and loops for processing all of them without repeating code. The Month 1 Boss asks you to prove all four weeks work together in one program.
learningObjectives: Create and iterate over arrays with loops
Create objects with multiple properties and access by key
Access and update nested properties
Combine arrays of objects to represent a real collection
Assemble variables, conditionals, functions, arrays, and objects into one multi-file program
weeks.expectedOutcome: A Personal JavaScript Toolkit - a working, multi-file command-line program using every Month 1 concept together to report on your own goals and projects.
stretchGoals: Add a `filter` or `find` call to search the projects array by status.
Add a second nested object (e.g., `settings`) inside userMemory and access a value two levels deep.
hints: Build the array first and confirm the loop prints every item before adding objects to it.
Accessing a missing property returns `undefined` silently, which is often more confusing than an error.
commonMistakes: Confusing an array's index (position) with a value stored inside it.
Relying on object property order for meaning, when order should never carry meaning.
Misspelling a property key on read, getting `undefined`, and mistaking it for missing data rather than a typo.
debugChecklist: If a loop skips the last item, check `<` vs `<=` against the array length.
If a property read is `undefined`, compare exact spelling and case to where it was defined.
Print the whole object with `console.log(obj)` before accessing one nested piece.
thinkingPrompts: Why is an array right for 'a list of projects' while an object is right for 'the details of one project'?
What goes wrong if you model a list of projects with only separate variables, like Week 2 did for one profile?
recallPrompts: How do you access the third item in an array called `projects`?
What are the two ways to access a property on an object?
weeks.missionReview: This week's boss mission tested whether four weeks of separate concepts can now work together, on demand, without relearning any of them. That's what 'foundation' actually means.
weeks.progressNotes: If splitting the boss mission across multiple files felt awkward, that discomfort is useful - Month 3's React components and Month 4's backend routes both depend on this instinct to separate concerns across files.
weeks.missionDebrief: Month 1 is complete. Every concept Elliot will ever use - variables, decisions, reusable logic, structured collections - now exists in your hands, proven by a program you wrote and can explain line by line.
weeks.commanderNotes: Look at your Week 1 first-run.js next to this week's boss toolkit. That gap is the real, measurable proof of a month's work - a fact you can scroll through on GitHub, not a feeling.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Month 2 moves Elliot out of the terminal and into the browser - the same logic you just mastered is about to become something you can actually click on.
reflectionPrompts: Explain, without using the words 'array' or 'object,' why you needed two different data shapes this week.
What broke first when you split the Boss Mission into multiple files, and what did fixing it teach you?
Across all four Month 1 weeks, which concept do you still feel least confident about, and what could you build tomorrow to test that gap?
If someone handed you a brand new problem right now, which Month 1 concept would you reach for first?
What is different about how you approach a JavaScript error today compared to Week 1?

months.description: The first month is where 'I understand code in theory' becomes 'I can make a computer do what I say, on my own machine, with my own hands.' You will not touch a database, a framework, or a phone this month - deliberately. Every mission strips away everything except the language itself: variables, decisions, functions, and the two data shapes (arrays and objects) that every later layer of Elliot is built from. If Month 1 goes well, nothing in Months 2-6 will feel like starting over; it will feel like adding a new room onto a foundation you already trust.
learningOutcome: Set up and verify a professional local development environment from scratch
Write, run, and debug JavaScript programs using the terminal and VS Code
Model real information (identity, goals, projects) using variables, strings, and numbers
Make a program branch and decide using conditionals and functions
Store and process collections of structured data using arrays, objects, and loops
Push every unit of work to GitHub with a README a stranger could follow
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 1 you will have shipped a Personal JavaScript Toolkit - a multi-file command-line program that models your own goals and projects and reports on them - built entirely from concepts introduced this month, with zero copied solutions.
months.motivation: Every professional JavaScript developer, backend engineer, and mobile developer still writes this exact vocabulary - variables, conditionals, functions, arrays, objects - every single day. Nothing here is 'beginner code' that gets replaced later; it is the permanent alphabet everything else in this bootcamp is written in.
months.recommendedPreparation: Have your laptop charged, a notebook for errors and commands, and your GitHub account ready before Week 1 begins. No prior JavaScript-specific experience is assumed - only comfort with what code, apps, and deployment are in theory.
months.careerInsight: In interviews for junior full-stack roles, the fundamentals in this month (closures, array methods, type coercion, `==` vs `===`) are the single most commonly tested topic. Mastering them now pays off at every hiring stage later.

concepts: The DOM as a tree of nodes
Running JS after the page loads
weeks.scenario: A static page can't be an assistant. This week Elliot's interface comes alive: JavaScript reaches into the page, finds specific elements, and changes their text on the fly. This is the exact mechanism behind every status update, every live counter, and every dynamic label you've ever seen in an app.
learningObjectives: Explain the DOM as a tree the browser builds from your HTML
Select elements reliably with querySelector
Change an element's text from JavaScript
Display live status values (mission, project, status)
Run script code at the right time relative to page load
weeks.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Status Panel that displays current mission, active project, and status - with the text set dynamically by JavaScript, not hard-coded in HTML - and a 'Last Updated' line.
stretchGoals: Add a button that cycles the status through several values.
Show the real current time in the 'Last Updated' line using `new Date()`.
hints: If `querySelector` returns `null`, the selector doesn't match anything - check the exact id/class spelling in the HTML.
A `#` prefix selects by id, a `.` prefix selects by class - mixing these up is the most common selector bug.
commonMistakes: Running DOM code before the element exists (script above the HTML it targets), so querySelector returns null.
Confusing `textContent` (safe, plain text) with `innerHTML` (parses HTML, riskier).
Selecting by the wrong prefix - `#` vs `.` - and getting null.
debugChecklist: Did querySelector return null? Log it to confirm.
Does the selector prefix match (id needs #, class needs .)?
Is the script running after the target element exists in the DOM?
Is the id/class spelled identically in HTML and JS?
Are there console errors pointing at the failing line?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser turn your HTML into a tree of objects instead of just displaying the text directly?
When Elliot eventually chats, how is 'add a new message to the screen' just a bigger version of what you did this week?
recallPrompts: What does querySelector return when nothing matches?
What is the difference between selecting with `#` and with `.`?
weeks.missionReview: You made a web page change because your JavaScript told it to. Every interactive product is just this - selection plus modification - repeated at scale.
weeks.progressNotes: The DOM is the single most important browser concept in this bootcamp. React (Month 3) exists specifically to make what you did this week easier - so this week is what makes React click.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's interface can now display live, JavaScript-driven data. Next week it will respond to the user, not just show information at them.
weeks.commanderNotes: If querySelector returning null frustrated you this week, good - that specific frustration is where real DOM intuition comes from.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week the page starts listening: buttons, clicks, and events turn your status panel into something the user can actually control.
reflectionPrompts: Explain the DOM in your own words to someone who has never heard the term.

How is updating status text this week related to how a chat app adds a new message?

hints: `addEventListener('click', fn)` takes the function itself - don't call it with `fn()` (which runs it immediately once).

commonMistakes: Passing `handler()` instead of `handler` to addEventListener, so it runs once at setup and never on click.

concepts: Rendering a saved list and deleting items
weeks.scenario: This is the week Elliot starts to remember. A form captures notes, localStorage saves them as JSON, and the notes survive a page refresh. This is Elliot's first real memory - the same read/write/persist pattern that every later notes, tasks, and knowledge feature is built on.
learningObjectives: Capture input values from a form
Prevent a form from reloading the page on submit
Save and load an array in localStorage using JSON
Render a saved list back to the page
Delete individual items and prevent empty entries
weeks.expectedOutcome: The Elliot Notes Vault: a browser app that saves notes to localStorage, renders them in a list, deletes individual notes, prevents empty notes, and keeps everything after a page refresh.
stretchGoals: Add note categories (learned / confused / next action) and filter by them.
Add an edit function that updates an existing note in place.
hints: localStorage only stores strings - you must `JSON.stringify` before saving and `JSON.parse` after loading.
A form submit reloads the page by default - call `event.preventDefault()` or your data vanishes instantly.
commonMistakes: Storing an object/array directly in localStorage without JSON.stringify, so it saves as the useless string '[object Object]'.
Forgetting preventDefault, so the page reloads on submit and appears to 'lose' the note.
Rendering notes once but not re-rendering after a save or delete.
debugChecklist: Are you JSON.stringify-ing before saving and JSON.parse-ing after loading?
Did you call event.preventDefault() on submit?
Does the notes array re-render after every save and delete?
Check localStorage in DevTools 'Application' tab - is the data actually there and valid JSON?
Are empty notes being rejected before save?
thinkingPrompts: Why does localStorage force you through JSON.stringify/parse instead of just storing your array directly?
How is this save/load/render loop the same one Elliot's backend will use in Month 4, just with a server instead of the browser?
recallPrompts: What two JSON functions convert between an object and a string?
What does event.preventDefault() stop from happening on a form submit?
weeks.missionReview: Elliot can now remember. The capture-store-render-persist cycle you built this week is the exact conceptual shape of every data feature for the rest of the bootcamp - it just moves to a server in Month 4.
weeks.progressNotes: This is the Month 2 boss week. If notes survive a refresh and you can explain why JSON.stringify was necessary, you've internalized browser persistence - a genuinely product-grade skill.
weeks.missionDebrief: Month 2 is complete: Elliot has an interface, responds to the user, and remembers data across sessions. Month 3 rebuilds all of this - faster and reusable - with React.
weeks.commanderNotes: The Notes Vault is your Month 2 flagship. When it survives a refresh with your notes intact, you've built Elliot's first real memory. That's a milestone worth screenshotting.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Month 3 begins with GitHub discipline and deployment, then introduces React - the tool that turns everything you built by hand this month into reusable components.
reflectionPrompts: Explain why localStorage forces you through JSON.stringify and JSON.parse.
What happened the first time you forgot preventDefault, and how did you diagnose it?
How is this save/load/render loop the same one Elliot's backend will use in Month 4?
What did you do to prevent empty or duplicate notes, and why does input validation matter?
Looking back at Month 2, how far has Elliot's interface come from the Week 5 static landing card?

months.description: Month 2 takes everything you can already do in a terminal and gives it a face. Elliot stops being text scrolling past in a console and becomes something you can see, click, and interact with in a browser. You'll structure interfaces with HTML, style them with CSS, make them respond to the user with the DOM and events, and - critically - make them remember data between page refreshes with localStorage. By the end, Elliot has its first real interface and its first browser-based memory.
learningOutcome: Structure a web interface with semantic HTML and style it responsively with CSS
Select and modify page elements dynamically using the DOM
Make a page respond to user actions with events and event listeners
Capture user input through forms and validate it
Persist structured data in the browser with localStorage and JSON
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 2 you will have shipped the Elliot Notes Vault: a browser app that captures notes through a form, saves them to localStorage, renders them back, and survives a page refresh - the first version of Elliot that remembers anything.
months.motivation: Every product a user actually touches is a DOM being manipulated by JavaScript in response to events. React (Month 3) is a faster way to do exactly what you'll do by hand this month - so doing it by hand once is what makes React make sense later instead of feeling like magic.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be fluent with Month 1's variables, functions, arrays, objects, and loops - the DOM is just those same tools pointed at a web page instead of a console.
months.careerInsight: 'Explain what the DOM is and how event delegation works' is a near-universal front-end interview question. The hands-on DOM work this month is where that answer comes from.

weeks.scenario: If it isn't saved, versioned, and shareable, it isn't proof. This week turns your practice into a public professional record: a clean repo, meaningful commits, a bug log, and - ideally - a deployed live link. This is the discipline that makes everything after it demonstrable to an employer.
learningObjectives: Stage, unstage, and commit changes deliberately

Structure a repository a stranger can navigate

weeks.expectedOutcome: A GitHub Mission Protocol repo with a clean structure, a README explaining the bootcamp, a commit log, a bug log, and at least three well-messaged commits - ideally with one project deployed live.

hints: `git status` before every commit shows exactly what you're about to save - make it a reflex.
A good commit message finishes the sentence 'This commit will...' - e.g., 'add delete button to notes vault'.

Committing everything in one giant commit instead of small, logical ones.
Never deploying, so the portfolio has no live, clickable evidence.
debugChecklist: Does `git status` show only the files you intend to commit?

Does the README let a stranger run the project?

concepts: Rendering fetched data to the DOM
weeks.scenario: Real products don't hard-code their data - they fetch it. This week Elliot learns to request JSON, wait for it without freezing, and render it as cards, handling the loading and error states that separate a real interface from a demo. This is the bridge between your front-end and Elliot's future backend.
learningObjectives: Read and reason about JSON data structures
Request data with fetch and handle the Promise with async/await
Show a loading state while data is in flight
Handle and display fetch errors gracefully
Render an array of fetched data as UI cards
weeks.expectedOutcome: A Resource Fetch Board that loads resources from a JSON file with fetch, shows a loading message, renders cards, handles errors, and optionally filters by type.
stretchGoals: Fetch from a real public API instead of a local JSON file.
Add a retry button that re-runs the fetch after an error.
hints: `await` only works inside an `async` function - marking the wrong function is the most common first error.
A fetch that 404s does NOT throw by default - you must check `response.ok` yourself.
commonMistakes: Expecting fetch to throw on a 404 - it resolves; you have to check response.ok manually.
Forgetting to `await` the fetch (or the `.json()`), so you get a Promise instead of data.
Never showing a loading state, so a slow fetch looks like a broken page.
debugChecklist: Is the function marked `async` where you use `await`?
Did you `await` both the fetch and the `.json()`?
Are you checking `response.ok` for non-200 responses?
Is the JSON path correct relative to the page?
Does the DevTools Network tab show the request and its status?
thinkingPrompts: Why doesn't JavaScript just freeze and wait for the data instead of using Promises?
What should the user see during the moment between requesting data and receiving it?
recallPrompts: What keyword must a function have to use `await` inside it?
Does fetch throw an error on a 404? What must you check instead?
weeks.missionReview: You made an interface that depends on data arriving over time - and handled the waiting and the failing. That's the exact skill every screen in Elliot's future backend-connected app needs.
weeks.progressNotes: Async thinking is a real conceptual step up. If loading and error states now feel like a requirement rather than an afterthought, you're thinking like a product engineer.
weeks.missionDebrief: You can now fetch and render data with proper loading/error handling. Next week React gives you a cleaner way to structure the interfaces that display it.
weeks.commanderNotes: The habit of always handling loading AND error states - not just the happy path - is what separates junior demos from shippable products. Build it now.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: React components and props. The cards you rendered by hand this week become reusable, composable building blocks.
reflectionPrompts: Explain async/await to someone who only knows synchronous code.
What was your first async bug (missing await, wrong async function, unchecked 404) and how did you find it?
Why is handling the loading state a product requirement, not a nice-to-have?
How does fetching from a local JSON file this week prepare you for calling Elliot's real backend in Month 4?
What does the DevTools Network tab reveal that console.log alone cannot?

weeks.scenario: The cards you rendered by hand in Month 2 become reusable building blocks this week. React components let you define a MissionCard or ProjectCard once and render it many times with different props - the exact structure Elliot's screens (chat bubbles, notes, project cards) are made of.
learningObjectives: Create a Vite React app and understand its structure
Write components that return JSX
Pass data into components with props
Compose small components into a larger UI
Render a list of components from an array
weeks.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Component Lab: a Vite React app with MissionCard and ProjectCard components receiving title/description/status props, rendering multiple cards from an array.
stretchGoals: Add a StatusBadge sub-component used inside the cards.
Give a card a default prop value for when data is missing.
hints: Every component must be exported and imported to be used - a forgotten export is the most common first error.
JSX uses `className`, not `class`, and every list-rendered element needs a unique `key`.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to export a component (or import it), causing a confusing 'element type is invalid' error.
Using `class` instead of `className` in JSX.
Rendering a list without a `key` prop, triggering a warning and subtle bugs.
debugChecklist: Is the component exported from its file and imported where used?
Are you using `className` not `class`?
Does every list item have a unique `key`?
Do the prop names match between where you pass and where you read them?
Does the browser console show a component error pointing to a file?
thinkingPrompts: How is a React component just a function that returns UI, given props as arguments?
Which pieces of Elliot's future interface are obviously 'a component rendered many times'?
recallPrompts: What must you do to a component before another file can use it?
Why does each item in a rendered list need a key?
weeks.missionReview: You built UI from reusable, prop-driven components. This is the mental model - small pieces composed together - behind every React app you'll ever build, including Elliot.
weeks.progressNotes: If props clicked as 'arguments to a UI function,' React will keep making sense. If they didn't yet, that's the one concept to solidify before adding state next week.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's interface is now componentized. Next week those components gain memory and interactivity through state.
weeks.commanderNotes: Props flow one way - down, from parent to child. Holding that single rule in mind prevents most early React confusion.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: React state. Your components stop just displaying props and start remembering and reacting to user input.
reflectionPrompts: Explain a React component as a function in your own words.
What was your first import/export error, and how did the message help (or not) you find it?
Which parts of Elliot's future UI do you now see as 'one component rendered many times'?
Why does React insist on a key for each list item?
How does building components compare to the hand-written HTML/DOM approach from Month 2?

weeks.scenario: Props display data; state remembers and changes it. This week Elliot's components come alive: a task console where users add, complete, and delete tasks, with the UI updating from state. This is the interactive core every Elliot screen - chat, notes, tasks - is built on.
learningObjectives: Add and update component state with useState
Build controlled inputs bound to state
Update arrays in state immutably (new array, not mutation)
Render, toggle, and delete list items
Derive a value (task count) from state
weeks.expectedOutcome: The React Task Console: add tasks via a controlled form, store them in state, mark complete, delete, show a live count, and validate empty input.
stretchGoals: Add all/active/completed filters.
Persist tasks to localStorage so they survive a refresh.
hints: Never mutate state directly - build a new array/object and pass it to the setter, or React won't re-render.
A controlled input's value comes from state and updates state on change - both directions must be wired.
commonMistakes: Mutating state directly (e.g., `tasks.push(...)`) instead of setting a new array, so the UI doesn't update.
Building an input whose value is set but whose onChange doesn't update state (or vice versa).
Forgetting a stable key on list items, causing incorrect re-renders when items change.
debugChecklist: Are you creating a NEW array/object for every state update, not mutating?
Is the input both reading from state (value) and writing to it (onChange)?
Does each task have a stable unique key?
Is the count derived from state, not tracked separately?
Does the console show any 'update during render' or key warnings?
thinkingPrompts: Why does React require a new array instead of letting you push to the existing one?
How is this task console structurally identical to Elliot's future notes and chat screens?
recallPrompts: What does useState return, and how do you update it?
Why must state updates be immutable?
weeks.missionReview: You built an interactive, stateful app where user actions change the UI through state. This is the Month 3 boss skill and the interaction model for every Elliot screen ahead.
weeks.progressNotes: Immutable state updates are the concept most new React developers fight. If 'new array, not mutate' is now a reflex, you're past the hardest part of React.
weeks.missionDebrief: Month 3 complete: you can build reusable, stateful, data-driven React interfaces. Month 4 gives them a backend to talk to.
weeks.commanderNotes: The Task Console is your Month 3 flagship. It's also, structurally, a preview of Elliot's task and notes screens - build it well and you're reusing it soon.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Month 4 opens with React Router (multi-page apps) and then builds Elliot's first real backend with Node and Express - the brain behind the interface.
reflectionPrompts: Explain why React needs immutable state updates instead of letting you mutate arrays directly.
What was your first 'the UI didn't update' bug, and what actually caused it?
How is this task console structurally the same as Elliot's future notes and chat screens?
What does a controlled input need wired in both directions, and why?
Looking back at Month 3, how has your idea of 'building an interface' changed since the hand-written DOM of Month 2?

months.description: Month 3 professionalizes how you build. It opens with GitHub discipline and deployment - turning private practice into public, shareable proof - then introduces fetch and asynchronous thinking (how apps talk to data), and finally React: the component-based library behind most modern product interfaces. By the end, everything you built by hand in Month 2 you can now build as reusable, stateful React components.
learningOutcome: Maintain a clean, documented GitHub repository and deploy a live app
Load and render external data asynchronously with fetch and JSON
Build reusable UI from React components and props
Manage interactive state with useState and render dynamic lists
Handle loading, error, and empty states like a professional
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 3 you will have shipped the React Task Console: a component-based app where users add, complete, and delete tasks with live state - the reusable interface foundation Elliot's screens are built from.
months.motivation: React is the single most in-demand front-end skill in the JavaScript job market, and it powers both Elliot's web app and (via React Native) its mobile app. Learning it on top of hand-built DOM work means you understand not just how to use it, but why it exists.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be comfortable with Month 2's DOM manipulation and events - React automates exactly that work, so knowing the manual version makes React's model intuitive rather than magical.
months.careerInsight: React fundamentals - components, props, state, keys, the rules of hooks - are the core of virtually every front-end technical interview. This month is your most directly employable skill set so far.

weeks.scenario: Elliot and your portfolio need more than one screen: home, projects, assistant, contact. This week you structure a real multi-page React app with routing and a shared layout - the navigational skeleton every future Elliot screen slots into.
learningObjectives: Install and configure React Router
Define routes for multiple pages
Build a reusable layout wrapping every page
Add navigation links with active styling
Keep the app mobile-friendly across pages
weeks.expectedOutcome: A Portfolio React Shell with Home, Projects, Elliot, and Contact routes, a shared MainLayout, active nav styling, and mobile-friendly pages.
stretchGoals: Add a 404 'not found' route for unmatched paths.
Add a nested route (e.g., a project detail page under /projects).
hints: A blank page after navigating usually means a mistyped route path - check the exact `path` string.
The shared layout should render the nav plus an <Outlet/> (or children) where each page appears.
commonMistakes: Mistyping a route path and getting a blank page instead of an error.
Duplicating the navbar on every page instead of putting it once in a shared layout.
Forgetting that a full browser refresh on a sub-route can 404 without correct host config.
debugChecklist: Do the route paths exactly match the link targets?
Is the layout wrapping all pages via Outlet/children?
Does the active link styling reflect the current route?
Does each page render on both navigation and refresh?
Any console errors from Router setup?
thinkingPrompts: Why does a single-page app need a router at all, when there's only one HTML page?
Which Elliot screens map to which routes, and what belongs in the shared layout vs. each page?
recallPrompts: What does a shared layout let you avoid repeating?
What usually causes a blank page after a route change?
weeks.missionReview: You built a real multi-screen app with shared structure. Every Elliot screen from here on lives inside this routing skeleton.
weeks.progressNotes: Routing is the point where a 'React exercise' starts feeling like a 'real app.' The layout-plus-pages pattern you built is exactly how Elliot's web client is organized in Month 6.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's front-end now has real navigation. Next week you build the other half of full-stack: a server that data can come from.
weeks.commanderNotes: Put anything shared (nav, footer, container) in the layout once. Repeating it per page is the mistake this week is designed to break you of.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: Node.js and Express. Elliot gets its first backend - a server that answers requests with JSON.
reflectionPrompts: Why does a single-page app still need a router?
What caused your first blank-page routing bug, and how did you fix it?
Which Elliot screens map to which routes, and what did you put in the shared layout?
How does a shared layout change how much code you repeat across pages?
What would break if you refreshed the browser on a deep route, and why?

weeks.scenario: Elliot needs a brain behind the interface. This week you build its first backend: a Node/Express server with health and profile endpoints that return JSON. This is the beginning of the server layer that will eventually store Elliot's notes, tasks, knowledge, and chat.
learningObjectives: Initialize an npm project and install Express
Create an Express server that listens on a port
Define GET routes that return JSON
Serve data from a JSON file
Explain the request/response cycle end to end
weeks.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Profile API: an Express server with GET /health and GET /profile returning JSON from a data file, runnable via an npm script.
stretchGoals: Add a GET /projects endpoint returning an array from a JSON file.
Add a simple request logger that prints each incoming request's method and path.
hints: `node server.js` starts the server; it keeps running until you stop it - a stopped server is why endpoints suddenly 'fail'.
Express sends JSON with `res.json(data)` - it sets the right headers for you.
commonMistakes: Testing an endpoint while the server isn't running and concluding the code is broken.
Forgetting to actually call `app.listen(port)`, so the server never starts.
Editing server code but not restarting the server, so old behavior persists.
debugChecklist: Is the server actually running (did app.listen fire, is the port free)?
Did you restart the server after editing it?
Is the route path spelled exactly as you're requesting?
Does the JSON file exist at the path server.js reads?
Does the terminal show the request arriving or an error?
thinkingPrompts: What happens, step by step, between your browser requesting /profile and receiving JSON?
Why must a server keep running, unlike a script that finishes and exits?
recallPrompts: What Express method sends a JSON response?
Why does a stopped server make every endpoint fail?
weeks.missionReview: You built a server that answers requests. Elliot now has the beginnings of a backend - the layer that will hold everything it remembers.
weeks.progressNotes: The request/response cycle is the mental model behind all backend work. If you can trace a request from browser to server to JSON and back, the rest of Month 4 builds smoothly.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot has a backend that serves data. Next week it learns to change data too, with full CRUD.
weeks.commanderNotes: 'It failed' at the backend usually means 'the server isn't running' or 'I didn't restart it.' Check those two first, every time.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: REST APIs and CRUD. Elliot's backend learns to create, read, update, and delete - the backbone of usable data.
reflectionPrompts: Trace a request from your browser to the server and back to JSON, in your own words.
What was your first 'endpoint failed' moment, and was it really the code or the server state?
Why must a server keep running while a plain script exits?
How is serving a JSON file here similar to and different from fetching one in Month 3?
What does the request/response cycle mean for how Elliot will eventually store your notes?

weeks.scenario: A backend that only reads is half a backend. This week Elliot's API learns full CRUD: create, read, update, and delete tasks, persisted to a JSON file. CRUD is the backbone of every usable data feature Elliot will have - notes, tasks, knowledge, all of it.
learningObjectives: Map CRUD operations to HTTP methods
Build GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE routes for a resource
Read a route parameter like :id
Parse JSON request bodies
Persist changes to a JSON file
weeks.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Tasks API with GET all, POST new, PATCH complete, and DELETE routes, file-based persistence, and validation that rejects empty tasks.
stretchGoals: Add input validation that returns a 400 with a clear message for bad requests.
Add a GET /tasks/:id route returning a single task or 404.
hints: Express needs `express.json()` middleware to read POST/PATCH bodies - without it, req.body is undefined.
Match the HTTP method to the intent: GET reads, POST creates, PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
commonMistakes: Forgetting express.json() middleware, so req.body is undefined on POST.
Using GET for actions that change data instead of POST/PATCH/DELETE.
Reading/writing the JSON file incorrectly so changes don't persist between requests.
debugChecklist: Is express.json() middleware registered before the routes?
Does each route use the correct HTTP method for its action?
Is :id parsed and matched correctly?
Are file writes actually saving (re-read to confirm)?
Do bad requests return a clear error, not a crash?
thinkingPrompts: Why does REST map different actions to different HTTP methods instead of one endpoint doing everything?
How is this tasks API the same shape as the notes API Elliot will also need?
recallPrompts: Which HTTP methods map to create, read, update, delete?
What middleware lets Express read a JSON request body?
weeks.missionReview: You built a full CRUD API with persistence. This is the single most reused backend pattern in the industry and the core of everything Elliot stores.
weeks.progressNotes: CRUD is the backbone skill of Month 4. If create/read/update/delete all persist correctly, you can build the data layer of almost any product.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's backend can now manage data fully. Next week you connect it to the React front-end for a complete round trip.
weeks.commanderNotes: Match methods to intent honestly - GET never changes data. That discipline is what makes an API RESTful and predictable.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: connect React to Express. The front-end and back-end finally talk, and Elliot becomes truly full-stack.
reflectionPrompts: Why does REST use different HTTP methods for different actions?
What was your first CRUD bug (missing express.json(), bad file write, wrong method) and how did you find it?
How is this tasks API the same shape as the notes API Elliot also needs?
What did you do to validate bad input, and why does the server never trust the client?
How does persisting to a file here foreshadow using a real database later?

concepts: Loading and error states across the stack
weeks.scenario: This is the week the two halves meet. Elliot's React client fetches, adds, and deletes tasks through the Express API - a complete full-stack round trip. Handling CORS, loading, errors, and a server-offline state is what makes it a real application rather than two disconnected demos.
learningObjectives: Run a React client and Express server simultaneously
Fetch backend data into React and render it
POST and DELETE from the UI and update state
Configure CORS for cross-origin requests
Handle loading, error, and server-offline states
weeks.expectedOutcome: The Elliot Web Client + API: a React app that reads and writes tasks through the Express backend, with loading/error states and a clear message when the server is offline.
stretchGoals: Add optimistic UI updates that revert if the request fails.
Extract the fetch logic into a small reusable API helper module.
hints: A CORS error in the console means the browser blocked a cross-origin request - enable CORS on the Express side.
Run the server and the client in two separate terminals; both must be up for the app to work.
commonMistakes: Seeing a CORS error and editing the front-end when the fix belongs on the server (enable CORS).
Only running one of the two processes and wondering why requests fail.
Not handling the server-offline case, so the UI hangs or shows a cryptic error.
debugChecklist: Are both the client and server running (two terminals)?
Is CORS enabled on the server for the client's origin?
Does the Network tab show the request, its status, and any CORS block?
Does the UI update after a successful POST/DELETE?
Is there a clear message when the server is down?
thinkingPrompts: Why does the browser block cross-origin requests by default, and why is CORS the intended fix rather than a hack?
Which parts of Elliot's data flow are now identical to how the final product will work?
recallPrompts: What does a CORS error actually indicate?
Why must both the client and server processes be running?
weeks.missionReview: You connected a real front-end to a real back-end with full data flow and honest error handling. Elliot is now a genuine full-stack application - the Month 4 boss achievement.
weeks.progressNotes: Full-stack connection is where many learners feel it 'all come together.' If tasks flow from the UI to the file and back, you've built the core of a real product.
weeks.missionDebrief: Month 4 complete: Elliot is full-stack - a React client talking to an Express API with persistence. Month 5 makes it reliable, installable, and mobile.
weeks.commanderNotes: CORS errors are a server-side fix, not a front-end one. Remembering that single fact will save you hours across the rest of the bootcamp.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Month 5: reliability, validation, PWA installability, a real mobile audit of TheScoreboard, and your first React Native app on your Samsung A70.
reflectionPrompts: Explain why the browser blocks cross-origin requests and why CORS is the right fix.
What was your first full-stack bug, and was it on the client or the server?
Which parts of this data flow are identical to how final Elliot will work?
How did you handle the server being offline, and why does that matter for a real product?
Looking back at Month 4, how does it feel to own both the interface and the server?

months.description: Month 4 gives Elliot a brain behind its face. You start by structuring a multi-page React portfolio with routing, then build your first real backend with Node.js and Express, design a REST API with full CRUD, and finally connect the React front-end to the Express back-end so data flows both ways. By the end, Elliot is a genuine full-stack application: a UI talking to a server that stores and serves data.
learningOutcome: Build a multi-page React app with client-side routing and shared layout
Create a Node.js/Express server that returns JSON
Design a REST API with GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE and file-based persistence
Connect a React front-end to an Express back-end across origins (CORS)
Handle loading, error, and offline states across the full stack
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 4 you will have a connected full-stack Elliot: a React web client that reads and writes tasks through an Express REST API with file-based storage - the backbone of the final product.
months.motivation: Full-stack ability - owning both the interface and the server - is what lets one person build a whole product. This month is where Elliot stops being a front-end demo and becomes a real application with a data layer.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be solid on Month 3's React state and fetch/async - the front-end half of full-stack builds directly on both, and Month 1's objects/JSON become your API payloads.
months.careerInsight: 'Can you build a CRUD API and wire a front-end to it?' is the single most common practical test in junior full-stack interviews and take-homes. This month is that exact skill, end to end.

weeks.scenario: Assistants must not silently fail. This week Elliot's settings panel learns to validate input, show clear errors, and recover gracefully - the reliability layer that makes a product trustworthy instead of fragile.
learningObjectives: Build a settings form with controlled inputs
Validate required fields before saving
Display clear error messages with an ErrorBanner
Persist valid settings and confirm they survive reload
Handle corrupted or invalid stored data without crashing
weeks.expectedOutcome: An Elliot Settings and Validation Panel that rejects empty name/weekly-hours input with a clear error, saves valid settings to localStorage, and recovers gracefully from invalid stored JSON.
stretchGoals: Add field-specific error messages instead of one generic banner.
Add a 'reset to defaults' action that clears corrupted settings safely.
hints: Validate before you save, not after - catching bad input early prevents it from ever reaching storage.
Wrap JSON.parse of stored data in try...catch; a corrupted string will otherwise crash the app on load.
commonMistakes: Saving invalid data first and only checking it later, letting bad state slip through.
Letting a JSON.parse failure throw uncaught and crash the whole app on load.
Showing a generic 'error' message that doesn't tell the user what to actually fix.
debugChecklist: Does validation run before any save?
Is JSON.parse wrapped in try...catch with a fallback?
Does the error message say specifically what's wrong?
Does reloading with valid settings show them correctly?
Does reloading with corrupted localStorage recover instead of crashing?
thinkingPrompts: Why should a settings panel never trust its own previously-saved data blindly?
How is this validation pattern the same one Elliot's backend will need for every API request?
recallPrompts: What does try...catch let you do that a plain function call doesn't?
Why validate before saving rather than after?
weeks.missionReview: You made a small product feature genuinely reliable - it can't be broken by bad input or corrupted storage. That reliability mindset now applies to everything else you build.
weeks.progressNotes: Validation and error handling are unglamorous compared to features, but they are what separates a demo from something you'd trust with real use. This is professional maturity, not busywork.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's settings are now trustworthy. Next week the whole portfolio becomes installable as a Progressive Web App.
weeks.commanderNotes: A product that never fails gracefully isn't more reliable - it's just untested. This week's forced failures make your app genuinely robust.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: Progressive Web Apps. Your portfolio becomes something a user can install on their home screen like a native app.
reflectionPrompts: Why should a settings panel never trust its own previously-saved data?
What corrupted-data scenario did you test, and how did your app recover?
How is form validation here the same pattern Elliot's backend will need for every request?
What's the difference between a generic error message and a genuinely useful one?

learningObjectives: Create and link a web app manifest
Set an app name, theme color, and icons

Document install steps for a user
weeks.expectedOutcome: A Portfolio PWA Upgrade: a manifest with name/icons/theme color, mobile-polished layout, documented install steps, and basic installability confirmed.

hints: The manifest must be linked with `<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">` in the HTML head - a missing link means no install prompt.
Icons need multiple sizes (192x192, 512x512 minimum) for installability checks to pass.
commonMistakes: Creating manifest.json but forgetting to link it in index.html, so the browser never sees it.
Using a single icon size, failing installability requirements.
Never actually testing installability, assuming the manifest alone is enough.
debugChecklist: Is the manifest linked in the HTML head?
Do the icon paths in the manifest actually resolve?
Are at least two icon sizes provided?
Does the manifest's start_url and scope make sense?
Have you tested at real mobile viewport width?

concepts: Improving an existing product vs. building fresh
weeks.scenario: TheScoreboard is a real-world training ground: an existing WordPress-based product, not a blank slate. This week you audit its mobile experience, test its REST API, and prototype a mobile-first improvement. This is a different, valuable skill from building fresh - most professional work is improving something that already exists.
learningObjectives: Audit a real product's mobile experience methodically
Understand and query the WordPress REST API
Design a mobile-first user flow
Build a small fetch prototype against a live external API
Document findings and a plan for someone else to act on
weeks.expectedOutcome: A TheScoreboard Mobile Audit + REST Prototype: at least 10 documented mobile UX observations, a mobile-flow plan, and a working fetch prototype against the WordPress REST API.
stretchGoals: Render fetched WordPress posts as styled cards in the prototype.
Propose a PWA improvement checklist specific to TheScoreboard.
hints: WordPress REST endpoints typically live under `/wp-json/wp/v2/posts` - confirm the exact base URL for the real site first.
A wrong or blocked endpoint often shows as a CORS error or 404 - both are useful, documentable findings, not just failures.
commonMistakes: Writing vague audit notes ('mobile is bad') instead of specific, actionable observations.
Giving up at the first failed fetch instead of documenting the exact error as a finding.
Designing an ideal mobile flow with no connection to what the REST API can actually provide.
debugChecklist: Is the WordPress REST base URL correct for this specific site?
Does a 404 or CORS error appear, and have you documented it as a finding?
Are your audit observations specific and actionable, not vague?
Does your mobile-flow plan reference real content the API can supply?
Would a teammate be able to act on your audit without more context?
thinkingPrompts: What's the difference between auditing your own new build and auditing someone else's existing product?
How does working within an existing system's constraints (its API, its content) change how you design?
recallPrompts: What's the typical base path for the WordPress REST API?
Name two things a good UX audit finding needs to include.
weeks.missionReview: You practiced a distinct professional skill: improving a real, existing product rather than building fresh. This is most of what working developers actually do.
weeks.progressNotes: This week intentionally has a different shape than most - more investigation and documentation, less pure building. That range is valuable; not every mission should feel identical.
weeks.missionDebrief: You've audited a real product and proven you can work with an existing API. Next week you leave the browser entirely for native mobile development.
weeks.commanderNotes: TheScoreboard is real-world training, not a distraction from Elliot. The audit-and-improve skill you practiced here is exactly what client and job work looks like.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: React Native and Expo. You'll run your first real mobile app on your own Samsung A70 - the last major skill before Month 6's full assembly.
reflectionPrompts: What's the difference between auditing an existing product and building something fresh?
What was your most useful (specific, actionable) audit observation, and why does it beat a vague one?
What did testing the WordPress REST API reveal - did it work as expected, and if not, what did you learn from the failure?
How did the API's real content shape your mobile-flow design?
How does this week's 'improve what exists' skill differ from every other week's 'build something new'?

concepts: Creating and running an Expo project
Core React Native components (View, Text, Button)
Expo Go and QR-code device testing
Live reload on a physical device
weeks.scenario: Elliot must live on your phone. This week you leave the browser for the first time and build a real mobile app with React Native and Expo, running live on your Samsung A70 - no heavy emulator required. This is the skill Elliot's mobile client is built on for the rest of the bootcamp.
learningObjectives: Set up the Expo development environment
Create a new Expo project
Run the app on a physical device via Expo Go
Understand View, Text, and Button as React Native's building blocks
Confirm live reload by editing App.js and seeing changes instantly
weeks.expectedOutcome: A Portfolio Mobile Shell v1: an Expo app with Home, Projects, and Elliot placeholder screens, running live on your Samsung A70, styled with basic React Native styling.
stretchGoals: Add simple navigation between the three placeholder screens.
Style each screen with a distinct accent color matching your portfolio brand.
hints: React Native has no HTML tags - `View` replaces `div`, `Text` replaces `p`/`span`; text must always be inside a `<Text>` component.
If the QR code won't connect, confirm your phone and laptop are on the same Wi-Fi network first.
commonMistakes: Trying to render raw text outside a `<Text>` component, which React Native rejects.
Assuming CSS class names work the same way - React Native uses StyleSheet objects, not CSS files.
Phone and laptop on different networks, so Expo Go can never find the dev server.
debugChecklist: Is all visible text wrapped in a `<Text>` component?
Are styles defined via StyleSheet.create, not CSS?
Are the phone and laptop on the same Wi-Fi network?
Does editing App.js trigger a live reload on the phone?
Does the terminal show the Expo dev server running without errors?
thinkingPrompts: Why does React Native need its own components (View, Text) instead of reusing HTML tags?
What does 'the same component model, a different rendering target' mean, comparing this to your Month 3 React work?
recallPrompts: What component must all visible text be wrapped in?
What must be true about your phone and laptop's network for Expo Go to connect?
weeks.missionReview: You ran real, native-feeling code on a physical phone for the first time. This is a genuine, resume-worthy mobile development milestone - not a simulation.
weeks.progressNotes: If View/Text/StyleSheet felt like 'React again, but different vocabulary,' that's exactly right - your Month 3 component instincts transfer directly to Expo.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot's mobile presence has begun. Month 6 turns these placeholder screens into a real mobile shell with navigation, storage, and a live backend connection.
weeks.commanderNotes: The moment your edit shows up live on your own phone is worth pausing on. That's the same reload loop you'll use to build Elliot's entire mobile app.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Month 6: mobile navigation and storage, a chat interface, knowledge and document handling, and finally, the full assembly of Elliot V1 across web, mobile, and backend.
reflectionPrompts: Why does React Native need its own components instead of reusing HTML tags?
What was your first React Native error, and how did it differ from a web React error?
How did it feel to see your own edit reload live on your physical phone?
What Month 3 React instincts transferred directly to this week, and what didn't?
Looking at Month 5 as a whole, how has your definition of 'reliable' and 'mobile-ready' changed?

months.description: Month 5 turns a working prototype into something closer to a real product. You harden the front-end and back-end against bad input and errors, make the portfolio installable as a Progressive Web App, apply mobile-product thinking to a real existing system (TheScoreboard), and - the big shift - leave the browser entirely and run your first React Native app on your own phone with Expo. By the end, you've practiced reliability, mobile UX auditing, and native mobile development in the same month.
learningOutcome: Validate input and handle errors gracefully on both client and server
Make a web app installable and mobile-friendly as a Progressive Web App
Audit an existing product's mobile experience and prototype against a real REST API
Set up Expo and run a React Native app on a physical Android device
Reason about product reliability and mobile UX like a professional, not just a student
months.milestoneDescription: By the end of Month 5 you will have a validated, installable Portfolio PWA, a documented TheScoreboard mobile audit with a working REST prototype, and your first React Native app running live on your Samsung A70 via Expo.
months.motivation: Reliability and mobile reach are what separate a demo from a product. This month is where Elliot's foundation gets trustworthy (validation, errors) and where you personally cross into native mobile development - the last major skill gap before Month 6's full assembly.
months.recommendedPreparation: Be comfortable with Month 4's React forms and Express APIs - validation this month hardens exactly that code, and Expo assumes basic React component fluency.
months.careerInsight: Mobile development (React Native/Expo) is a distinct, well-paid specialization on top of web React skills. Getting a real app running on a physical device this month is a concrete, resume-worthy milestone most self-taught web developers never reach.

weeks.scenario: Elliot mobile needs chat, notes, tasks, settings, and profile screens - not just one placeholder view. This week you add real navigation and on-device storage, giving Elliot's mobile app the same memory its web app has, but native.
learningObjectives: Set up navigation between multiple mobile screens
Build a working Notes screen
Persist notes using device-appropriate local storage
Pass and read data across screens
Test persistence by reloading the app on the phone
weeks.expectedOutcome: Elliot Mobile Notes v1: Home, Notes, and Settings screens connected by navigation, with notes saved locally, listed, and deletable, surviving an app reload.
stretchGoals: Add a note-editing flow that updates an existing note in place.
Add simple screen transition animations.
hints: Mobile local storage is asynchronous - always `await` reads and writes, unlike synchronous `localStorage` on the web.
Navigation libraries expect screens to be registered in a navigator - a screen not registered won't be reachable.
commonMistakes: Treating mobile storage as synchronous like localStorage, causing race conditions where data isn't ready yet.
Forgetting to register a new screen in the navigator, making it unreachable.
Not testing persistence by actually closing and reopening the app, only checking within one session.
debugChecklist: Are all storage reads/writes properly awaited?
Is every screen registered in the navigator?
Does data persist after fully closing and reopening the app, not just navigating away?
Do screen transitions work in both directions?
Any red-screen errors from a broken import?
thinkingPrompts: Why is mobile local storage asynchronous when browser localStorage isn't?
How is this Notes screen structurally the same as Month 2's web Notes Vault, and what's genuinely different?
recallPrompts: Why must mobile storage reads/writes be awaited?
What must you do before a screen becomes reachable via navigation?
weeks.missionReview: Elliot's mobile app now has real structure and memory - multiple screens, on-device persistence, the same conceptual shape as its web counterpart.
weeks.progressNotes: If this felt like 'Month 2's Notes Vault again, but mobile and async,' that recognition is exactly the point - you're reusing your own mental models across platforms.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot mobile has navigation and memory. Next week it gains a voice: a chat interface shared conceptually across web and mobile.
weeks.commanderNotes: Always await mobile storage. The bugs that come from forgetting are timing bugs - the hardest kind to spot by just reading the code once.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: the chat interface. Elliot starts to feel like an assistant, on both web and mobile.

weeks.scenario: A real assistant product is not just screens - it talks back. This week Elliot gets a chat interface on both web and mobile: a message list, an input, a send action, and a mock assistant reply. This is the interaction pattern the whole product has been building toward.
learningObjectives: Model chat messages as an array of objects
Render user and assistant messages distinctly
Build a controlled input with a send action
Add a mock assistant response on send

weeks.expectedOutcome: Elliot Chat UI v1: a chat window (web and mobile) that renders message history, accepts new input, sends it, shows a mock assistant reply, and auto-clears the input.
stretchGoals: Add a typing indicator shown briefly before the mock reply appears.
Style user and assistant bubbles with distinct colors and alignment.
hints: Give every message a stable unique id (not the array index) for its React key - array-index keys break when messages are added.
Auto-scroll to the newest message after each send so the conversation reads naturally.
commonMistakes: Using the array index as the key, causing subtle bugs when messages are added or reordered.
Not clearing the input after send, so users accidentally resend the same text.
Forgetting to distinguish user vs. assistant messages visually, making the conversation unreadable.
debugChecklist: Does every message have a stable unique id used as its key?
Does the input clear after sending?
Are user and assistant messages visually distinct?
Does the list auto-scroll or stay readable as it grows?
Does sending an empty message get rejected?
thinkingPrompts: Why is a stable message id better than the array index as a React key here?
What would change about this chat UI once it talks to a real backend instead of a mock reply?
recallPrompts: Why shouldn't you use array index as a list key for chat messages?
What should happen to the input field immediately after sending a message?

weeks.progressNotes: This is one of the most satisfying missions in the bootcamp because it 'feels like Elliot.' Notice how much of the hard work (state, lists, controlled inputs) was already learned in Month 3 - this week mostly applies it.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot can hold a conversation shape, even with mock replies. Next week the replies get real: knowledge, uploads, and basic understanding.
weeks.commanderNotes: This is the mission most learners screenshot first. It's the moment Elliot stops looking like an exercise and starts looking like a product.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Next week: knowledge and uploads. Elliot's replies stop being mocked and start coming from real data you give it.

What would change about this chat UI once it talks to a real backend instead of a mock reply?

concepts: Returning a rule-based answer from matched knowledge
weeks.scenario: This is where Elliot becomes more than screens. The assistant must answer based on personal data, projects, notes, tasks, and documents - not mocked replies. This week you build a knowledge endpoint, accept uploaded or pasted text, search it for matches, and return a real, basic answer.
learningObjectives: Structure personal/project facts as searchable JSON
Build an endpoint that serves knowledge data
Accept pasted text or an uploaded file from the client
Implement basic keyword search over stored knowledge
Return a rule-based answer derived from a match, not a mock
weeks.expectedOutcome: Elliot Knowledge + Upload Prototype: a /knowledge endpoint, a web Upload page accepting pasted or uploaded text, keyword search over the knowledge base, and a basic real answer returned from a match.
stretchGoals: Attempt basic PDF text extraction with a free library (e.g., pdf-parse).
Rank multiple keyword matches by relevance instead of returning the first.
hints: Start with plain pasted text before attempting file upload or PDF extraction - get the search logic right on simple input first.
A basic keyword search (does the knowledge text include the query term?) is a legitimate V1 - it does not need to be AI-powered.
commonMistakes: Attempting PDF extraction before plain-text search even works, debugging two hard problems at once.
Building a search that only matches exact, full-sentence queries instead of simple keyword presence.
Not handling the 'no match found' case, leaving the user with silence instead of a clear response.
debugChecklist: Does plain pasted-text search work before you add file/PDF handling?
Does the search match on individual keywords, not just exact phrases?
Is there a clear response when no match is found?
Does an unsupported file type fail gracefully with a message, not a crash?
Does the /knowledge endpoint return valid JSON?
thinkingPrompts: Why is a simple keyword search a legitimate, honest V1 rather than a compromise to be embarrassed about?
What does 'basic understanding' honestly mean for Elliot V1, versus what a full AI system would do?
recallPrompts: What's the minimum viable version of 'document understanding' this week builds?
Why build plain-text search before attempting PDF extraction?
weeks.missionReview: Elliot can now answer from real data you gave it - not a mock. This V1 honesty (keyword search, not full AI) is a deliberate, correct product decision, not a shortcut.
weeks.progressNotes: This week's non-goal is as important as its goal: V1 does not need perfect AI. A working, honest, rule-based search is real progress and real shipped value.
weeks.missionDebrief: Elliot has a first real knowledge feature. Next week everything - web, mobile, backend, chat, knowledge - gets assembled and shipped as V1.
weeks.commanderNotes: Resist the urge to over-build 'real AI' here. A working keyword search that returns an honest answer beats an ambitious feature that never ships.
weeks.nextMissionTeaser: Final week: feature freeze, full web and mobile integration, deployment, and your graduation demo. Elliot V1 comes together.
